headline: Meta open sources Muse Gadgets for custom AI hardware development
summary: Developers can now use open-source firmware and a Linux SDK to build their own hardware devices that connect to Meta's personal AI agent, Muse.
details: Meta has launched Muse Gadgets, an open-source project allowing developers to build custom hardware connected to its personal AI agent, Muse. This initiative provides open-source firmware and a Linux SDK, along with initial project ideas like e-ink displays or HDMI stick integrations.

The project supports low-cost hobbyist computers such as Raspberry Pi and ESP32 boards. Users can connect Muse to various components like displays, buttons, sensors, and actuators, enabling broad customization. Meta has also established a Discord channel for community support.

Meta itself developed a gadget called Muse Home Link, a USB-C powered device that connects Muse to a home network and smart devices. The company produced 5,000 Home Links and offered them free to Muse subscribers, with high demand noted by Nat Friedman.

Muse Gadgets is part of Meta's larger strategy to expand Muse beyond a standalone chatbot, targeting wider integration. This includes Muse for Small Business, offering free access with usage limits and connections to tools like Shopify and Slack, and a new Meta Enterprise Platform.

topic: federal bill to ban flock cameras
headline_marked: Sanders introduces bill to [[ban federal government from using Flock]] and all ALPR systems
headline: Sanders introduces bill to ban federal government from using Flock and all ALPR systems
summary: The "Ban Flock Act" would bar federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers and penalize states that don't comply.
details: Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced the "Ban Flock Act," aiming to prohibit federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) or accessing data from local police and private companies. This bill, while titled after Flock, applies to all ALPR systems.

The proposed legislation includes exceptions only for toll collection and future Congress-approved uses, which would limit data retention to 48 hours. It also mandates financial penalties for state and local governments that fail to ban the technology.

If enacted, state and local governments would lose grants from five federal departments, including the Justice Department and Homeland Security, unless they cease using ALPRs. Americans could also sue the federal government for violations.

Flock is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., with over 120,000 cameras processing more than 20 billion vehicle reads monthly. The company has recently tightened its rules, reducing default data retention to seven days from 30.

Flock also introduced an audit tool to flag unusual searches, locking officers out pending review. This comes after high-profile abuse cases, such as a former Milwaukee officer misusing the platform for personal reasons.
The bill is co-sponsored by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Jeff Merkley, though it faces long odds in Congress.
